synopsis: EgoScale learns dexterous robot policies from action-labeled egocentric human video, then aligns them with robot sensing and control using a small human–robot play dataset. A vision-language backbone conditions a flow-based action expert predicting wrist motion and hand joints. Real-robot success improves after both human pretraining and aligned mid-training; transfer still requires robot demonstrations and embodiment-specific adaptation.

problem.text: Human video scales more readily than dexterous robot teleoperation, but noisy motion estimates and different hand kinematics obstruct transfer. EgoScale asks whether explicit wrist and finger supervision at large scale provides a useful manipulation prior, and how much aligned robot experience is then needed.

contributions.text: A 20,854-hour human pretraining mixture combines diverse egocentric recordings with higher-precision EgoDex motion supervision.
Human pretraining and aligned mid-training are complementary; task-specific post-training completes the deployment recipe.
Validation loss tracks downstream completion across five data scales; one-shot and G1 experiments suggest transferable manipulation structure within the tested settings.

inputs: Egocentric RGB observations and language instruction; robot proprioception when available.
Human wrist/hand estimates supply training labels; a learned token substitutes for missing human proprioception.
outputs: Chunks of relative wrist/end-effector poses and hand joint targets, decoded for the active embodiment.

steps.name: Build explicit action labels
steps.detail: Estimate camera motion with SLAM and hand pose from 30-FPS video. Transform the wrist into a world frame, then express motion relative to the chunk reference. Retarget hand keypoints to 22-DoF Sharpa joints.

steps.name: Constrain hand retargeting
steps.detail: Appendix D uses URDF kinematics and joint limits in per-frame nonlinear optimization with CasADi/IPOPT. Warm-start from the previous solution and apply exponential smoothing. Objective terms, weights and filter coefficient are unspecified.

steps.name: Condition the action expert
steps.detail: Image/language embeddings condition a DiT trained by flow matching. Embodiment-conditioned MLPs encode state/noisy actions and decode hand actions; the backbone, expert and wrist representation are shared.

steps.name: Align sensing before adaptation
steps.detail: Mid-training covers 344 tabletop tasks, approximately 30 human and 5 robot trajectories each: about 50 human hours and 4 robot hours. Matched cameras, calibrated intrinsics, Vive wrist tracking and Manus hand capture narrow the domain gap.

training.text: Stage I updates all VLA parameters for 100K steps on 256 GB200 GPUs, global batch 8,192, learning rate 5×10⁻⁵.

Stage II runs 50K steps, batch 2,048, learning rate 3×10⁻⁵. The vision-language backbone is frozen while the separately named vision encoder and DiT update; Appendix D.1 also lists state/action adapters.

Stage III uses robot task demonstrations for 10K steps, batch 512, learning rate 3×10⁻⁵. The vision encoder is frozen after mid-training and unfrozen otherwise. The introduction’s two-stage transfer description thus becomes three optimization stages including post-training.

inference.text: The VLM conditions iterative action generation from noisy inputs; Figure 2 labels N iterations without specifying N. End-effector and joint targets control the R1Pro arms/hands with RGB feedback; its base and torso remain fixed.
On G1, EgoScale supplies upper-body targets; a separately trained Homie controller handles lower-body balance and locomotion. No rollout of predicted future images or world states is described.

equations.explanation: T is camera-to-world pose; H is a camera-frame hand-keypoint transform, index 1 denoting the wrist. W is world-frame wrist pose. The written relative transform uses chunk time 0, although nearby prose and Appendix D.1 call it consecutive/frame-to-frame motion; the implementation convention is unresolved.

Equation (1) fits validation MSE L against data quantity D, described as hours, with reported R²=0.9983. Literal hours and these coefficients do not reproduce Figure 5’s plotted losses. Normalization/precision is unresolved; this formula should not support extrapolation.

results.setting: Shirt rolling, card sorting, tong fruit transfer, bottle unscrewing and syringe transfer; 100 robot demonstrations each except 20 for shirt. Two seeds; nominally 10 trials per checkpoint, with conflicting bottle counts.
results.metric: Average binary success rate; average task completion score
results.comparison: No pretrain: 0.02/0.24; midtrain only: 0.28/0.53; human pretrain: 0.38/0.71 (success/completion).
results.interpretation: The plotted success gain is 54 percentage points, clarifying the abstract’s “54%.” Card success decreases from 0.70 human-only to 0.65 combined.

results.setting: Pretrain on 1k, 2k, 4k, 10k or 20k hours, then directly post-train on robot tasks.
results.comparison: Validation uses 2,000 held-out human episodes, 20 sampled timesteps each, averaging 16 action chunks per timestep before MSE.
results.interpretation: The within-range association supports scaling, but does not separate behavioral diversity from hours or establish performance beyond 20k hours.

results.task: One-shot shirt folding and water-bottle unscrewing
results.setting: One robot plus 100 aligned human demonstrations for folding; the same allowance per bottle for three geometries.
results.value: Figure 6: 0.88 folding and 0.556 bottle; prose reports bottle as 0.55.
results.interpretation: “One-shot” counts robot demonstrations. The text’s blanket baseline-failure claim conflicts with nonzero folding success in the chart.

results.setting: 7-DoF tri-finger hands; G1 play during mid-training and downstream adaptation. Two seeds, 10 trials per seed as stated.
results.metric: Binary success for Pen in Bin / Dish in Rack
results.interpretation: Plotted gains are 37 and 30 percentage points. This is adapted transfer; 0.67 is not straightforwardly compatible with the stated two-by-ten binary-trial denominator.

results.setting: Card, tong and bottle; wrist-only versus fingertip trajectories with an MLP joint mapping versus retargeted joints.
results.metric: Task completion score, ordered Card / Tong / Bottle
results.interpretation: Joint targets perform best here, but the fingertip condition changes the mapping mechanism as well as supervision.

limitations.text: Bottle evaluation conflicts: Section 3.1 calls it Task III with 16 trials; Appendix B calls it Task IV and says four configurations, four trials each, but 12 total. One-shot additive rubrics can exceed their stated unit maximum; milestone exclusivity/normalization is missing. G1 dish increments sum to 0.99 although the maximum is called 1.0.

Figures 4–8 omit error bars and seed-level outcomes. Small evaluations with controlled initial scenes limit uncertainty and generalization conclusions. Figure 8’s bottle joint score is 0.61 versus human-only 0.63 in Figure 4, without explanation.

Joint model/data scaling, weaker unlabeled supervision and zero-shot novel-task execution remain future directions. Diverse human training scenes do not themselves establish broad robot deployment coverage.

reproduction.text: Reproduction requires the human mixture including 829 EgoDex hours, aligned collection, task demonstrations, calibration and hand URDFs. Appendix A specifies an OAK-D-Wide head camera and two OAK-1-Wide wrist cameras; training compute is given without a complete executable configuration.

Missing details include exact checkpoint/model size, action horizon, inference iterations/control rate, mixture weights, filtering thresholds, split identities, optimizer schedule, retargeting weights and software versions. Clarify the 21-versus-25 keypoint wording, wrist reference convention and G1 adaptation data quantity.

Reader-proposed checks: isolate aligned mid-training at fixed data/update budgets, and compare action representations under controlled decoder and label-quality protocols. Predeclare binary success and report per-seed outcomes; neither check was run.

reasoning.text: VLA, dual-system VLM/DiT architecture and post-training/data augmentation are supported. However, “Latent action pretraining” misdescribes explicitly supervised wrist poses and joints: internal embeddings do not establish latent-action discovery. Prediction paradigm and quadrant being not applicable are supported because the policy predicts actions without a described future-state model.

discussionQuestions: Does matched sensing or shared motion structure account for more of the mid-training benefit?
Would validation MSE retain its predictive ranking under new robot tasks and a different diversity mix?
How much of the joint-target advantage comes from retargeting constraints rather than the prediction space?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title block, arXiv margin, Abstract and Introduction
evidence.detail: Exact EgoScale title and 15-author list; NVIDIA, University of California, Berkeley and University of Maryland. Margin states arXiv:2602.16710v1, 18 Feb 2026; header states 2026-2-19. Abstract says success improves by 54%.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Figure 1 and caption; p. 5, Section 2.4
evidence.detail: Figure 1 depicts pretraining, mid-training and post-training while its caption calls the transfer framework two-stage; Section 2.4 explicitly specifies three optimization stages.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section 2.1, Raw Sensor Streams, Wrist-level Arm Motion and Hand Articulation
evidence.detail: Defines camera/world transforms, 21 keypoints, wrist index 1 and chunk-reference relative wrist transform; retargets to 22-DoF Sharpa joints. Prose calls wrist changes consecutive despite the time-0 equation.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 3–4, Section 2.2, Stage I
evidence.detail: 20,854 total hours, diverse in-the-wild scenes, 30-FPS RGB, off-the-shelf SLAM/hand estimation, and 829 EgoDex hours covering 194 tasks. Precise processing configuration and mixture sampling weights are not supplied.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Figure 2(a), caption and Section 2.2, Stage II
evidence.detail: 344 tasks, about 30 human and 5 robot trajectories each, 50 human and 4 robot hours. Matching cameras/intrinsics, Vive wrist poses and Manus 25-joint transforms synchronized with video.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Figure 2(b) and caption; p. 5, Section 2.3
evidence.detail: VLM encodes image/language; DiT uses flow matching for action chunks. Figure shows noisy joint/EEF inputs and an N-iteration loop. Missing human proprioception uses a learnable placeholder; embodiment input/output MLPs surround shared modules.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 2.4
evidence.detail: Stage I: 100K steps, 256 GB200 GPUs, batch 8,192, learning rate 5e-5, all parameters trainable. Stage II: 50K, batch 2,048, 3e-5; backbone frozen, vision encoder/DiT updated. Stage III: 10K, batch 512, 3e-5; vision freezing depends on prior mid-training.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 2.5
evidence.detail: R1Pro base/torso fixed; two 7-DoF arms receive relative end-effector commands; 22-DoF Sharpa hands receive joint targets. Head and two wrist RGB cameras supply observations.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Section 3.1, Tasks and Evaluation Metric
evidence.detail: Five tasks use 100 demonstrations except shirt rolling with 20. Two training seeds, nominally 10 trials per checkpoint, image-overlay initialization. Bottle-specific four-by-four exception is labeled Task III.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Figure 4(a–b), Average, Card and Bottle groups; Sections 3.2–3.3
evidence.detail: Average completion/success: no pretrain 0.24/0.02, mid-only 0.53/0.28, human-only 0.71/0.38, combined 0.83/0.56. Card success 0.70 human-only versus 0.65 combined. Bottle human-only completion 0.63. Scaling checkpoints omit mid-training.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Figure 5, Section 3.3 and Eq. (1); p. 9, opening continuation
evidence.detail: Completion at 1k/2k/4k/10k/20k hours is 0.30/0.45/0.48/0.57/0.71. Validation averages 16 samples at each of 20 timesteps from 2,000 episodes. Fit L=0.024−0.003 ln(D), R²=0.9983 defines D as hours, inconsistent with plotted losses under literal substitution. Continuation disclaims extrapolation.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Figure 6 right-hand charts, caption and Section 3.4
evidence.detail: One robot plus 100 aligned human demonstrations per object; three water bottles. Folding success mid-only/human-only/combined: 0.15/0.35/0.88; bottle: 0/0/0.556. Completion: 0.25/0.65/0.92 and 0.10/0.10/0.64. Prose gives bottle 0.55 and overstates baseline failure. Related motions exist in mid-training.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 9–10, Section 3.5 and Figure 7
evidence.detail: G1 has 7-DoF tri-finger hands. Combined completion 0.83/0.88 and success 0.67/0.50 for Pen in Bin/Dish in Rack; mid-only completion 0.45/0.54, human-only 0.68/0.58; both baselines success 0.30/0.20. Text states two seeds, 10 trials each and Homie lower-body control.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Figure 8; p. 11, Section 3.6
evidence.detail: Card/Tong/Bottle completion: wrist-only 0.56/0.24/0.26, fingertip 0.17/0.76/0.55, joints 0.74/0.79/0.61. Fingertip predicts wrist/fingertip SE(3) trajectories then maps to joint commands with an MLP. Authors describe unstable grasps and mapping errors.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Section 6, final paragraph
evidence.detail: Model/data scaling, weaker/unlabeled video objectives and possible zero-shot novel-task execution are future directions.

evidence.location: PDF p. 13, Appendix A, Figure 9 and caption
evidence.detail: R1Pro uses Sharpa hands; G1 uses tri-finger hands. Both have two OAK-1-Wide wrist cameras and an OAK-D-Wide head camera.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 13–14, Appendix B, R1 Pro Sharpa rubrics
evidence.detail: Completion uses task-specific progress or additive milestones. Tong uses lemon/plum, five trials each. Bottle is Task IV: four configurations, four trials each, but 12 total stated. Syringe has seven additive substeps.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 14–15, Appendix B, Tasks VIII–IX and binary-success definition
evidence.detail: Folding adds 0.4, 0.4, 0.3 with messy-fold penalty. Bottle lists 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 0.2, 0.2. Naive addition exceeds the stated [0,1] range; milestone exclusivity/normalization is unspecified. Binary success requires end-to-end completion.

evidence.location: PDF p. 15, Appendix B, G1 Tasks
evidence.detail: Pen in Bin is described as marker/canister manipulation. Dish assigns 0.11 per pickup, transfer and placement for three plates but calls the maximum 1.0; literal sum is 0.99.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 15–17, Appendix C.1–C.5 and Figure 10
evidence.detail: Long-tailed category, environment, task and object distributions. Category/environment/task plots show groups above 50 hours. Broad human coverage is not a robot generalization evaluation.

evidence.location: PDF p. 17, Appendix D and D.1 Shared Wrist Action
evidence.detail: Text says 21 human keypoints represented as 25, and 20 robot keypoint poses. Optimizes 22 joints with URDF limits, CasADi/IPOPT, previous-frame warm start and exponential smoothing; objectives/weights/filter settings absent. D.1 calls wrist changes frame-to-frame.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 17–18, Appendix D.1
evidence.detail: Embodiment-specific state/noisy-action encoders and joint decoders surround shared VLM/DiT. G1 play participates in mid-training; vision encoder, expert and state/action adapters update while vision-language backbone is frozen. G1 data quantity and detailed adapter configuration are absent.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 7–10, Figures 4–8; pp. 13–18, Appendices A–D.1
evidence.detail: Main results, one-shot, G1 transfer and action ablation appear as plots. The supplied paper contains no quantitative result table; appendices provide prose rubrics, system images and dataset plots.
